svg.text: Vascular emergency · the 6 Ps · Rutherford categories · embolus vs thrombus · ESVS 2020
Sudden fall in limb perfusion threatening viability (onset < 2 weeks). A surgical emergency — irreversible muscle necrosis after ~6 h
of complete ischaemia; peripheral nerves are hit even earlier.
Paraesthesia + paralysis (sensorimotor deficit) mark a threatened limb needing emergency revascularisation. Pain easing as sensation
is lost is ominous — not improvement.
AF, post-MI mural thrombus, valve, aneurysm (AAA /
plaque rupture at a stenosis; graft occlusion
I / IIa → anticoagulate, or thrombolysis / surgery · IIb → emergency surgical revascularisation (embolectomy / bypass) ± on-table
lysis · III → primary amputation (reperfusion may be fatal). *arterial Doppler often (IIa) / usually (IIb) inaudible.
Give IV unfractionated heparin at diagnosis unless contraindicated (limits propagation). Do NOT delay theatre for imaging in
Rutherford IIb. Keep the limb dependent and warm — never actively heat.
K+, H+, lactate, myoglobin from ischaemic muscle
monitor K+ / ECG / CK; IV fluids; treat hyperkalaemia;
reperfusion oedema in tight fascial compartments (calf
pain on passive stretch, tense compartments, pain out
thrombosis / distal embolisation; bilateral; associated AAA
aortic bifurcation — bilateral ALI + buttock involvement
massive iliofemoral DVT — venous; swollen, blue leg
young, active, no atherosclerotic risk factors
systemic features; aortic dissection with malperfusion
punctate digital ischaemia with preserved pulses
Rutherford IIb is limb-threatening — straight to theatre; don't lose time on imaging or slow thrombolysis.
Pain easing while the limb goes numb signals progressing nerve death, not recovery.
Venous Doppler stays audible until category III — loss of BOTH arterial and venous signals = irreversible: amputate, don't
Always give IV heparin at diagnosis and hunt the source — check for AF, echo, and the contralateral pulses.
Suspect a thrombosed popliteal aneurysm when ALI is paired with a prominent or aneurysmal contralateral popliteal.
Anticipate reperfusion: hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria / AKI and compartment syndrome — keep a low fasciotomy threshold.
ESVS 2020 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Acute Limb Ischaemia (Björck, Earnshaw et al., Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2020;59:173–218).
